title: Do Patients Who Report High Satisfaction Actually Experience Meaningful Improvement in Functioning, Autonomy and Quality of Life? A Narrative Review
content: Background. Patient satisfaction is among the most widely collected and most consequential metrics in health care, embedded in reimbursement, public reporting and quality improvement, and frequently treated as a proxy for the care a patient received. Yet satisfaction is an expectation-anchored appraisal of an encounter, whereas functioning, autonomy and quality of life are states of the person. Whether the two move together determines whether satisfaction-weighted quality frameworks reward better outcomes or merely met expectations. Methods. We conducted a narrative review, searching MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and Web of Science to 31 August 2026 for evidence linking patient satisfaction or patient experience to functioning, autonomy or quality of life. We included psychometric and conceptual work on satisfaction measurement; observational and administrative studies relating experience to clinical quality, safety and utilisation; specialty evidence from elective arthroplasty, spine surgery, chronic pain and rehabilitation; trial and systematic review evidence on patient-reported outcome feedback, autonomy support and activation; and theoretical work on response shift and the disability paradox. Disconfirming evidence was sought explicitly. Results. The evidence is mixed and strongly context-dependent. Positive experience is often, though not consistently, associated with better clinical processes; a substantial countervailing literature reports null, domain-specific or inverse associations, including higher utilisation, expenditure and mortality, and satisfaction discriminates technical quality poorly. Divergence is clearest in elective surgery: satisfaction after total knee arthroplasty is 82–89% while 8–15% report frank dissatisfaction with function, up to 28% are dissatisfied despite high aggregate success, and fulfilment of expectations predicts satisfaction in 93% of arthroplasty studies whereas preoperative expectations predict it in only half. Satisfaction tracks present state rather than magnitude of change. In rehabilitation, 88% of patients who missed their functional goals were nonetheless satisfied, and functional gain ranked below family involvement, goal attainment, communication and pain control as a correlate of satisfaction. Autonomy support, patient activation and goal-anchored care relate more consistently to functional and quality-of-life outcomes than satisfaction does. Response shift, the anchoring of minimal important difference estimates to satisfaction, and the disability paradox further weaken the inference from satisfaction to improvement. Conclusion. High satisfaction is not a reliable surrogate for meaningful improvement in functioning, autonomy or quality of life. Satisfaction should be retained and repositioned as a distinct patient-evaluation outcome, reported alongside — never instead of — directly measured functioning, autonomy and quality of life. Frameworks dominated by satisfaction risk rewarding expectation-driven, low-value care while concealing the patients whose outcomes are worst.
